## Two Independent Means {#sec-independent-means}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-6
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")
pricing <- read.csv(data_path("pricing_sales.csv"))
discount <- pricing$sales[pricing$strategy == "Discount"]
bundle <- pricing$sales[pricing$strategy == "Bundle"]
hp <- read.csv(data_path("headphone_prices.csv"))
online <- hp$price[hp$channel == "Online"]
physical <- hp$price[hp$channel == "Physical"]

# Pooled two-sample t, rounded as in the book
pooled <- function(m1, v1, n1, m2, v2, n2) {
  sp2 <- round(((n1 - 1) * v1 + (n2 - 1) * v2) / (n1 + n2 - 2), 4)
  se <- round(sqrt(sp2 * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2)), 4)
  list(sp2 = sp2, se = se, df = n1 + n2 - 2, d = m1 - m2, t = round((m1 - m2) / se, 3))
}
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Tell independent samples from paired samples by how the data were collected.
2. Use the $F$ test to choose between the pooled $t$ test and the Welch $t$ test.
3. Carry out the pooled $t$ test and CI by hand, and read both tests from R.

### Concept

Two **independent** random samples are drawn from two populations, for
example stores using two pricing strategies, or graduates of two universities.
We estimate $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ by $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$. Its standard error
depends on whether the two population variances are equal:

- **Equal variances** ($\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$): combine the two sample
  variances into one **pooled variance** $s_p^2$ and use the **pooled $t$ test**
  with df $= n_1 + n_2 - 2$. This is calculated by hand.
- **Unequal variances**: use the **Welch $t$ test**. Its df is not a whole
  number, so we read it from R.

So the method has a first step: compare the variances with the $F$ test of
Section 3.5.

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Choosing the method

1. Paired or independent? (Section 3.4) If paired, use the paired $t$ test.
2. If independent, test $H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ (two-sided, $\alpha$ = 0.05).
   - accept $H_0$ → **pooled $t$ test**: `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)`
   - reject $H_0$ → **Welch $t$ test**: `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)`
:::

### Formulas and Conditions

**Conditions:** two independent random samples; both populations approximately normal.

**Pooled method** (equal variances), df $= n_1 + n_2 - 2$
$$
s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2},
\qquad
\text{SE} = \sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}
$$
$$
\text{CI: } (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\,\text{SE}
\qquad
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\text{SE}}
$$

**Welch method** (unequal variances): read $t_{\text{cal}}$, df, p-value and CI from `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)`.

| $H_1$ | Critical region (pooled) |
|:---:|:---|
| $\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$ | $t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha/2,\,\text{df}}$ or $t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha/2,\,\text{df}}$ |
| $\mu_1 < \mu_2$ | $t_{\text{cal}} < t_{\alpha,\,\text{df}}$ |
| $\mu_1 > \mu_2$ | $t_{\text{cal}} > t_{1-\alpha,\,\text{df}}$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-6
n1 <- length(discount); n2 <- length(bundle)
m1 <- round(mean(discount), 4); m2 <- round(mean(bundle), 4)
v1 <- round(var(discount), 4); v2 <- round(var(bundle), 4)
P <- pooled(m1, v1, n1, m2, v2, n2)
t95 <- crit_t(.95, P$df); t975 <- crit_t(.975, P$df); me <- t975 * P$se
fv <- var.test(discount, bundle)
tg <- t.test(discount, bundle, var.equal = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
tt <- t.test(discount, bundle, var.equal = TRUE)
```

### Example: Pooled $t$ Test

**Example 3.6.1.** A retail chain tries two pricing strategies. `r n1`
stores use a **discount** strategy and `r n2` other stores use a **bundle**
strategy. Daily sales (units) are recorded:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pricing
#| tbl-cap: "Daily sales (units) under two pricing strategies"
knitr::kable(data.frame(Strategy = c("Discount", "Bundle"),
                        Sales = c(paste(discount, collapse = ", "), paste(bundle, collapse = ", ")),
                        n = c(n1, n2), Mean = c(num(m1), num(m2)), Variance = c(num(v1), num(v2))))
```

(a) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, check whether the variances are equal.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether mean sales are higher with the discount strategy.
(c) Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_D - \mu_B$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

The stores are different stores, so the samples are independent.

**(a)** $H_0: \sigma_D^2 = \sigma_B^2$ vs $H_1: \sigma_D^2 \ne \sigma_B^2$.
$F_{\text{cal}} = `r num(v1)`/`r num(v2)` = `r fmt(v1 / v2, 3)`$; from `var.test()` below,
p-value = `r fmt(fv$p.value, 4)` $\ge$ 0.05, so we accept $H_0$: the variances are
equal. Use the **pooled** method.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu_D = \mu_B$ $\quad H_1: \mu_D > \mu_B$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.**
$$
s_p^2 = \frac{`r n1 - 1`(`r num(v1)`) + `r n2 - 1`(`r num(v2)`)}{`r n1` + `r n2` - 2} = `r num(P$sp2)`
$$
$$
\text{SE} = \sqrt{`r num(P$sp2)`\left(\frac{1}{`r n1`} + \frac{1}{`r n2`}\right)} = `r num(P$se)`
$$
$$
t_{\text{cal}} = \frac{`r num(m1)` - `r num(m2)`}{`r num(P$se)`} = `r fmt(P$t, 3)`,
\qquad \text{df} = `r P$df`
$$

**Step 4: p-value.** From the R output, p-value = `r fmt(tg$p.value, 4)`.
(With the table: $t_{0.95,\,`r P$df`} = `r fmt(t95, 3)`$, critical region $t_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(t95, 3)`$.)

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value = `r fmt(tg$p.value, 4)` <
$\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is, mean daily sales are higher with
the discount strategy than with the bundle strategy at the 0.05 level of significance.

**(c)** $t_{0.975,\,`r P$df`} = `r fmt(t975, 3)`$:
$`r num(P$d)` \pm `r fmt(t975, 3)`(`r num(P$se)`) = `r num(P$d)` \pm `r num(me)`$.
95% CI: (`r fmt(P$d - me, 2)`, `r fmt(P$d + me, 2)`). We are 95% confident that the
difference in mean daily sales (discount $-$ bundle) is between
`r fmt(P$d - me, 2)` and `r fmt(P$d + me, 2)` units.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## One-sided test, two-sided interval

The one-sided test in (b) rejects $H_0$, but the 95% CI in (c) contains 0. This
is not a contradiction: the CI matches a **two-sided** test, whose p-value
(`r fmt(tt$p.value, 4)`) is twice the one-sided p-value.
:::

### Reading R Output

```{r}
#| label: r-data-pricing
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("discount", discount), vec_code("bundle", bundle))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-pricing
#| echo: !expr show_code
var.test(discount, bundle)
t.test(discount, bundle, var.equal = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
t.test(discount, bundle, var.equal = TRUE)
```

With `var.equal = TRUE` R prints **Two Sample t-test** (pooled); with
`var.equal = FALSE` it prints **Welch Two Sample t-test**. Check the title before reading the numbers.

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-6-welch
hv <- var.test(online, physical)
hw <- t.test(online, physical, var.equal = FALSE)
```

### Example: Welch $t$ Test

**Example 3.6.2.** A consumer researcher records the price (baht) of the
same model of headphones at `r length(online)` online stores and
`r length(physical)` physical stores. Is the mean price
different?

```{r}
#| label: r-data-headphones
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("online", online), vec_code("physical", physical))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-headphones
#| echo: !expr show_code
var.test(online, physical)
t.test(online, physical, var.equal = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

**Equal variances?** p-value of the $F$ test = `r fmt(hv$p.value, 4)` < 0.05,
so we reject $H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$. Online prices vary much more.
Use the **Welch** test (the second output).

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: \mu_{\text{online}} = \mu_{\text{physical}}$ $\quad H_1: \mu_{\text{online}} \ne \mu_{\text{physical}}$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(hw$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r fmt(hw$parameter, 2)`

**Step 4: p-value.** p-value = `r format(signif(hw$p.value, 4))` (= `r format(round(hw$p.value, 6), scientific = FALSE)`), which is < 0.0001

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.** p-value < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject
$H_0$. That is, the mean price is different online and in physical stores at the
0.05 level of significance; since $\bar{x}_{\text{online}}$ = `r big(mean(online))`
< $\bar{x}_{\text{physical}}$ = `r big(mean(physical))`, it is lower online.

We are 95% confident that the difference in mean price (online $-$ physical)
is between `r big(hw$conf.int[1])` and `r big(hw$conf.int[2])` baht.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-6
set.seed(2757)
uni_A <- round(rnorm(10, 24.5, 3.2), 1)
uni_B <- round(rnorm(12, 22.3, 3.0), 1)
ya_m <- round(mean(uni_A), 4); yb_m <- round(mean(uni_B), 4)
ya_v <- round(var(uni_A), 4); yb_v <- round(var(uni_B), 4)
YP <- pooled(ya_m, ya_v, 10, yb_m, yb_v, 12)
yv <- var.test(uni_A, uni_B); yt <- t.test(uni_A, uni_B, var.equal = TRUE)
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.6.1

The starting monthly salaries (thousand baht) of 10 economics graduates from
University A and 12 from University B are compared:
$\bar{x}_A$ = `r num(ya_m)`, $s_A^2$ = `r num(ya_v)`, $\bar{x}_B$ = `r num(yb_m)`,
$s_B^2$ = `r num(yb_v)`.

(a) Use the first output to decide which $t$ test to use.
(b) Calculate $t_{\text{cal}}$ by hand (it is hidden in the output).
(c) Use the R output to test whether the mean starting salaries are different at $\alpha$ = 0.05.
:::

```{r}
#| label: r-data-uni
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("uni_A", uni_A), vec_code("uni_B", uni_B))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-3-6
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| eval: false
var.test(uni_A, uni_B)
t.test(uni_A, uni_B, var.equal = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: r-yt-3-6-out
print(var.test(uni_A, uni_B))
mask_print(t.test(uni_A, uni_B, var.equal = TRUE), list(c("^t = ", 1)))
```

::: {.workspace lines="6"}
:::

::: {.workspace steps="names" method="pvalue"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.6.1"}
**(a)** $F$ test p-value = `r fmt(yv$p.value, 4)` $\ge$ 0.05: accept equal
variances, so use the pooled $t$ test.

**(b)** $s_p^2 = \dfrac{9(`r num(ya_v)`) + 11(`r num(yb_v)`)}{20} = `r num(YP$sp2)`$,
SE $= \sqrt{`r num(YP$sp2)`(1/10 + 1/12)} = `r num(YP$se)`$,
$t_{\text{cal}} = (`r num(ya_m)` - `r num(yb_m)`)/`r num(YP$se)` = `r fmt(YP$t, 3)`$.

**(c)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B \quad H_1: \mu_A \ne \mu_B$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(yt$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r yt$parameter`

**Step 4.** p-value = `r fmt(yt$p.value, 4)`

**Step 5.** p-value = `r fmt(yt$p.value, 4)` $\ge$ $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we accept
$H_0$. That is, the mean starting salaries of graduates from the two
universities are equal at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### Formula Summary

| Situation | Method | R |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Paired data | paired $t$ on $d$ (Section 3.4) | `t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE)` |
| Independent, equal variances | pooled $t$: $s_p^2 = \dfrac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}$, $t_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_p^2(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}$, df $= n_1+n_2-2$ | `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)` |
| Independent, unequal variances | Welch $t$ | `t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)` |
| CI (pooled) | $(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2) \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\,\text{SE}$ | two-sided output |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-6-exercises
set.seed(2758)
north <- round(rnorm(14, 9.2, 2.6), 1)
south <- round(rnorm(16, 7.4, 0.9), 1)
ev <- var.test(north, south)
ep <- t.test(north, south, var.equal = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
ew <- t.test(north, south, var.equal = FALSE, alternative = "greater")
```

### Exercises

**3.6.1** An economist compares the monthly inflation expectations (%) reported
by `r length(north)` firms in the North and `r length(south)` firms in the South. She wants to know whether expectations are higher in the
North. Three outputs are shown.

```{r}
#| label: r-data-region
#| echo: !expr show_code
#| code: !expr c(vec_code("north", north), vec_code("south", south))
```

```{r}
#| label: r-ex-3-6
#| echo: !expr show_code
cat("Output 1\n"); var.test(north, south)
cat("Output 2\n"); t.test(north, south, var.equal = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
cat("Output 3\n"); t.test(north, south, var.equal = FALSE, alternative = "greater")
```

(a) Which of Output 2 and Output 3 should she use? Explain.
(b) Write the decision and interpretation at $\alpha$ = 0.05.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.6.1"}
(a) In Output 1 the p-value = `r fmt(ev$p.value, 4)` < 0.05, so the variances are
not equal. Use the Welch test, Output 3. (Output 2 assumes equal variances.)

(b) $H_0: \mu_N = \mu_S \quad H_1: \mu_N > \mu_S$. From Output 3,
$t_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(ew$statistic, 3)`$, df = `r fmt(ew$parameter, 2)`,
p-value = `r fmt(ew$p.value, 4)` < $\alpha$ = 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. That is,
mean inflation expectations are higher in the North than in the South at the
0.05 level of significance.
:::

**3.6.2** For each study, say whether you would use the paired $t$ test or a
two-sample (pooled or Welch) $t$ test.

(a) The rice yield of 15 farms is recorded before and after an irrigation project.
(b) The household income of 60 randomly chosen households in Chiang Mai is compared with that of 60 randomly chosen households in Bangkok.
(c) For each of 12 provinces, the unemployment rate of men is compared with that of women.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.6.2"}
(a) Paired (same farms twice). (b) Two-sample: two independent samples; check
the variances with the $F$ test to choose pooled or Welch. (c) Paired (men and
women are matched within each province).
:::
